This notebook expands the second unit of the course. The lecture slides are a map; this text is the territory. Unit 1 ended with a classifier "trained" by computing two means; this unit asks what training means in general — what it is for a machine to learn — and answers as a definition (Section 1), as a step in the practice of data science (Section 2), as a family of paradigms (Sections 3–5) and as an algorithm you can run by hand (Sections 6–7). The official plan omits regression, the simplest learning problem and the one in which model, loss, optimisation and overfitting can be seen without distraction; regression is therefore the core of this unit, and logistic regression — a regression model used as a classifier — is the first classifier studied properly. Every figure and number in the text is produced by code you can see and change.

Learning objectives

  • State Mitchell's definition of learning, identify task, performance and experience in a clinical problem, and distinguish inductive from deductive inference.
  • Define data science, structured and unstructured data and the seven steps of a project, and locate machine learning within them.
  • Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, semi- and self-supervised learning with a biomedical example of each; use "class", "label" and "target" correctly.
  • Define a classifier and its decision boundary, and relate the statistical, neural and evolutionary approaches to Unit 1.
  • Derive and solve the normal equations, interpret coefficients, R² and residuals; implement gradient descent and explain the learning rate; recognise overfitting and explain ridge.
  • Explain the sigmoid, log-loss and threshold of logistic regression, compute one probability by hand, and extend to several classes.
  • Say what k-means and value iteration learn, and from what.

How to read this notebook

Read linearly once, executing each code cell and reading the paragraph that interprets it; then return by section. Green boxes are exercises that change one thing in the cell above; blue boxes key ideas; orange boxes misconceptions; purple boxes links to other units or to BGM324. Only numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy and scikit-learn are used, all pre-installed in Colab; the datasets ship with scikit-learn. Supplement S0 covers the toolkit, Supplement S1 the evaluation methodology previewed in Section 11.

1. What it means to learn

1.1 Mitchell's definition

The field's operational definition of learning is Tom Mitchell's:[1]

Definition (Mitchell, 1997)

A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E.

It is purely behavioural, and it turns "does the system learn?" into three concrete questions every application paper should answer.

Component Question Breast-cancer example (Unit 1) Hospital-ward example
Task T What is the system to do? Assign malignant or benign to an aspirate described by 30 nuclear features Predict whether a patient will deteriorate within 24 h
Performance P How is doing well measured? Agreement with the biopsy (better: the two error rates separately) Sensitivity at a fixed false-alarm rate
Experience E What data does it see? 569 labelled aspirates from Wisconsin Vital signs and outcomes of past admissions

The idea predates the definition. In 1959 Arthur Samuel's checkers program improved by playing against itself and adjusting the weights of its evaluation function; he called it "machine learning": programming computers to learn from experience so as to eliminate much of the detailed programming.[2] The shift from expert systems to learned systems (Unit 1) is the shift from writing the rule to writing the procedure that finds the rule.

1.2 The three ingredients of a learning algorithm

Every learning algorithm in this course is built from three parts:

  1. A model (hypothesis space): a family of functions $f_\theta$ indexed by parameters $\theta$ — intercept and slope for a line, millions of weights for a network; the algorithm can only find a member of the family.
  2. A loss function $L(\theta)$: how badly $f_\theta$ performs on the training data — squared errors, misclassifications, negative log-probability of the labels; it operationalises Mitchell's $P$.
  3. An optimiser: the search for the parameters minimising the loss — a closed formula (Section 6), iterative descent (Section 7) or evolutionary search (Section 4, Unit 7).

Domingos compresses this into learning = representation + evaluation + optimisation; his dozen further lessons — generalisation is what counts, data alone are not enough, overfitting has many faces — this unit illustrates one by one.[3]

Common misconception

"Training" is not "programming the answer". The human supplies the form (model), the criterion (loss), the data and the labels; the algorithm finds the parameters. When a model "was trained on 100,000 X-rays", nobody wrote the rule that reads the X-ray, and nobody may be able to read it.

1.3 Inductive and deductive inference

Learning in Mitchell's sense is inductive inference: from particular observations to a general rule. Deductive inference goes the other way, and the two differ in every respect that matters:

Deductive Inductive
Direction general → specific: rules to cases specific → general: cases to a rule
Role apply knowledge someone already has discover knowledge from data
Guarantee conclusion certain if the premises are true conclusion probable, never certain
Risk rigidity: fails on cases the rules did not anticipate over-generalisation: a rule that fits the sample, not the world
In AI expert systems, logic (Unit 1, Section 3.1) machine learning (this course)

"All mammals have lungs; a whale is a mammal; therefore a whale has lungs" is deduction: certain, contained in the premises. "Every mammal examined so far has lungs; therefore all mammals have lungs" is induction: how the rule was obtained, fallible in principle and reliable in practice. Rats learn inductively: one that falls ill after a novel bait avoids that bait — and that flavour — thereafter, which is why poisoned baits fail against rats so quickly. A spam filter shows both in software. A deductive filter stores every message marked as spam and blocks exact copies: it never makes a false accusation and is defeated by one changed character. An inductive filter learns which words characterise the marked messages and scores new ones by them: it generalises to messages never seen, and is sometimes wrong. Memorisation is deduction from a table; learning is induction to a rule, and the methodology of this course exists because induction is fallible and its reliability must be measured.

2. From data science to machine learning

2.1 What data science is

Data science extracts knowledge and actionable conclusions from data by combining statistics, computing and domain knowledge; its roots are in statistics, and Donoho's historical account asks what is genuinely new in it.[4] Machine learning is the part of data science that builds models which learn from data; data science also includes everything before (asking the question; collecting, cleaning and exploring the data) and after (interpreting and communicating). It follows the scientific method — observe, question, collect data designed to answer it, analyse, conclude, communicate so others can check — at a scale classical experimentation did not face. In a real project model fitting takes a small fraction of the time; the rest goes to the data.

2.2 Kinds of data and where they come from

Structured data conform to a predefined data model — a table with fixed columns and types, as the data matrix of Unit 1 — and live in relational databases queried with SQL and, institutionally, in a data warehouse, a curated store built for known analyses. Unstructured data have no predefined model — clinical notes, images, audio, sequences — and live as files or in NoSQL databases and, at scale, in a data lake of raw data interpreted only when read. Most hospital data are unstructured, and the pattern-recognition pipeline of Unit 1 is the machinery that turns them into the structured table every method here requires. Quantitative data admit arithmetic; qualitative data are categories, text or judgements (Unit 1, Section 4.4 refines this). Analysis methods are named by their product: classification (a category), regression (a number), clustering (groups without labels) and data mining, the discovery of patterns such as association rules (Section 3.3).

Data come from transactional systems (hospital, pharmacy, laboratory records), public sources (statistics, repositories such as UCI), experiments and trials, curated databases (ChEMBL, DrugBank, UniProt), the literature and patents, sensors (monitors, wearables, imaging) and media. Each carries its own biases (Unit 1, Section 4.6).

2.3 Purposes

Projects describe a phenomenon (how many patients were readmitted), explain it (which factors are associated), predict it (which patients will be readmitted) and, downstream, reduce cost, mitigate risk and improve efficiency. Machine learning serves mainly prediction.

2.4 The seven steps of a data-science project

  1. Problem identification. The question, the unit of analysis, the target, the measure of success, the decision informed — Mitchell's $T$, $P$, $E$.
  2. Data collection. From the sources above, with a legal basis (Unit 1, Section 7) and documented provenance.
  3. Data cleaning. Quantify missing data and decide (discard, impute, model); detect outliers and judge them; remove unwanted records and columns; unify structure and format.
  4. Exploratory data analysis (EDA). Descriptive statistics, univariate and multivariate (correlations, cross-tabulations); hypothesis tests where warranted; above all graphical representation.
  5. Feature engineering. Attribute selection; class balance; grouping of categories; normalisation (Section 7 shows why); feature correlations, since correlated features destabilise linear models (Section 6.5).
  6. Machine-learning prediction. Choose, fit, evaluate honestly (Section 11, Supplement S1), iterate back to steps 3–5.
  7. Data storytelling. Communicate figures, uncertainty and limitations to the people who will act, in their language.

Three cells illustrate steps 3–5 on the breast-cancer data,[5] loaded here for the whole notebook; since the shipped data are clean, the first cell deletes 5 % of the values at random.

# Step 3, data cleaning: quantify missing values (injected here for illustration) and flag outliers by z-score.
cancer = datasets.load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
X, y = cancer.data, cancer.target                      # y: 0 = malignant, 1 = benign
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X_dirty = X.mask(rng.random(X.shape) < 0.05)           # delete 5 % of the cells at random -> NaN
missing = X_dirty.isna()
print(f"cells missing: {missing.to_numpy().mean():.1%} | rows with at least one missing value: {missing.any(axis=1).mean():.1%} "
      f"| rows that would survive 'drop any row with a NaN': {(~missing.any(axis=1)).sum()} of {len(X)}")
print("columns with most missing values:", missing.sum().sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).to_dict())

z = (X - X.mean()) / X.std()                           # z-scores of the clean data
outlier_rows = (z.abs() > 4).any(axis=1)
print(f"values beyond 4 standard deviations: {(z.abs() > 4).to_numpy().sum()} in {outlier_rows.sum()} patients; "
      f"the most extreme is '{z.abs().max().idxmax()}' at z = {z.abs().max().max():.1f}")

cells missing: 5.1% | rows with at least one missing value: 80.0% | rows that would survive 'drop any row with a NaN': 114 of 569
columns with most missing values: {'mean smoothness': 44, 'mean area': 37, 'mean texture': 36}
values beyond 4 standard deviations: 67 in 34 patients; the most extreme is 'concavity error' at z = 12.1

With 5 % of cells missing at random, 80 % of rows have a gap and dropping incomplete rows would keep 114 patients of 569 — which is why imputation is normal practice and missingness is quantified per column. The z-score screen flags 67 values beyond four standard deviations in 34 patients; whether they are errors or extreme tumours is for the pathologist to judge.

# Step 4, exploratory data analysis: univariate summaries by class and the correlation structure of the features.
means = X.join(y.rename("benign")).groupby("benign").mean().T
means.columns = ["malignant mean", "benign mean"]
means["ratio M/B"] = means["malignant mean"] / means["benign mean"]
print("features that differ most between the classes (ratio of class means):")
print(means.sort_values("ratio M/B", ascending=False).head(5).round(3).to_string())

corr = X.iloc[:, :10].corr()                            # the ten 'mean' features
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.2))
im = ax.imshow(corr, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_yticks(range(10))
ax.set_xticklabels([c.replace("mean ", "") for c in corr.columns], rotation=60, ha="right", fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticklabels([c.replace("mean ", "") for c in corr.columns], fontsize=8)
for i in range(10):

        ax.text(j, i, f"{corr.iloc[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5, color="w" if abs(corr.iloc[i, j]) > 0.6 else "k")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label="Pearson correlation"); ax.set_title("Correlation between the ten 'mean' features")

Figure 1. Pearson correlation between the ten "mean" features. Radius, perimeter and area correlate at 0.99 or above — three measures of nuclear size — and concavity with concave points at 0.92. # Step 5, feature engineering: class balance, standardisation, and removing redundant features.
print(f"class balance: {np.bincount(y)[0]} malignant ({(y == 0).mean():.1%}), {np.bincount(y)[1]} benign ({(y == 1).mean():.1%})")
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
scaled = pd.DataFrame(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X), columns=X.columns)
summary = pd.DataFrame({"raw mean": X.mean(), "raw sd": X.std(), "scaled mean": scaled.mean().round(10), "scaled sd": scaled.std()})
print(summary.loc[["mean radius", "mean area", "mean smoothness", "mean fractal dimension"]].round(3).to_string())

# drop one of every pair of features correlated above 0.95 (keep the first)
full_corr = X.corr().abs(); drop = set()
for i, a in enumerate(full_corr.columns):
    for b in full_corr.columns[i + 1:]:
        if full_corr.loc[a, b] > 0.95 and a not in drop: drop.add(b)
print(f"features dropped as redundant (|r| > 0.95 with a kept feature): {len(drop)} of 30 -> {sorted(drop)[:6]} ...")

                        raw mean   raw sd  scaled mean  scaled sd
mean radius               14.127    3.524         -0.0      1.001
mean area                654.889  351.914         -0.0      1.001
mean smoothness            0.096    0.014          0.0      1.001

The classes are 37 % malignant and 63 % benign: mild enough to need no correction, but a classifier that always says "benign" is already 63 % accurate, the baseline every reported accuracy must beat. Standardisation gives every feature mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so that mean area (raw standard deviation 352) and mean smoothness (0.014) enter distance- and gradient-based methods equally. The redundancy screen drops six of thirty features. None of this is "machine learning", and all of it affects the result more than the choice among the classifiers of Section 5.

Data science versus machine learning

Machine learning is step 6 of seven. A project excellent at step 6 and careless at steps 1, 3 or 7 answers the wrong question, learns the artefacts of its data, or is never used. The methods of this course are necessary, not sufficient.

3. The paradigms of learning

The paradigms differ in the kind of feedback contained in the experience $E$, not in the algorithm.

Figure 2. Left: supervised — every input comes with the correct output and the learner fits a function between them. Centre: unsupervised — the same inputs without labels; two groups are visible, and k-means (Section 10) will find them. Right: reinforcement — no dataset at the outset; an agent acts, observes the new state and a scalar reward, and discovers by trial and error which actions lead to high cumulative reward.

3.1 Supervised learning

The experience is pairs $(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)$: input and correct output, supplied by a "supervisor" — a pathologist, a laboratory, a follow-up visit. The task is a function with $f(\mathbf{x}) \approx y$ on unseen inputs. A categorical $y$ makes it classification; a numerical $y$ (progression, glucose, survival time) makes it regression. They share everything but the loss and the output, so Sections 6–8 do regression and Section 9 turns the machinery into a classifier. Labels encode exactly what we want predicted, which is why most practical impact is supervised; their cost — a radiologist's time, a biopsy, a year of follow-up — is the paradigm's limit.

Terminology: class, label, target

In classification class and label are synonyms for the category predicted; target covers both. In regression the target is a continuous value and should not be called a class — there are no classes in a regression problem, and the slides' use of "class" for the regression output is a slip. Say target or response for regression, class or label for classification.

3.2 Two examples from chemistry

Two problems from computational drug discovery — the research field of the laboratory that prepared this material, and the subject of the QSAR unit of BGM324 — show both forms. The instances are molecules and the features are descriptors computed from the structure: molecular weight (MW), hydrogen-bond donors (HBD) and acceptors (HBA), and polar surface area (PSA) — the descriptors of Lipinski's "rule of five" for oral absorption (MW < 500, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10; PSA < 140 Å² in later refinements).[6]

Classification: is the molecule an approved drug? A binary label — FDA-approved or not — assembled from fda.gov, DrugBank[7] and the Drug Repurposing Hub (clue.io); given the descriptors of a new molecule, predict it.

Regression: how potent is it? The IC50 of a compound against a target is the concentration at which it inhibits the target's activity by 50 %; the lower, the more potent, so compound A with IC50 = 10 µM is a better inhibitor than compound B with 1000 µM. Measured values for millions of compound–target pairs are curated in ChEMBL[8] and BindingDB. Because IC50 spans orders of magnitude, the usual target is pIC50 = −log10(IC50 in mol/L): 10 µM is 5, 1 µM is 6, one unit is tenfold in potency, and the errors become closer to Gaussian.

The cell reproduces both tables with illustrative values (right ranges, not measured compounds). Each follows the workflow of every supervised method: a training step, in which molecules with known labels or pIC50 are given to the algorithm, which adjusts a model's parameters to reproduce them; and a prediction step, in which the descriptors of a new molecule are fed to the fitted model, which outputs a predicted label or pIC50.

Compound A (pIC50 = 5) beats B (pIC50 = 3) by two orders of magnitude. Real QSAR models use hundreds of descriptors — the situation ($p$ comparable to $n$) in which the regularisation of Section 8 becomes unavoidable.

3.3 Unsupervised learning

The experience is the inputs alone, $\{\mathbf{x}_i\}$. With no correct answer to approximate, the task is reformulated as finding structure, and the slides name four sub-types, each a part of Unit 5. Clustering groups instances by similarity (Figure 2, centre; Section 10.1). Dimensionality reduction replaces the $p$ features by a few new ones that retain most of the variation — principal components, or the two-dimensional embeddings used for single-cell data. Feature selection keeps a subset of the original features; its motivation is the curse of dimensionality: at fixed sample size, adding features first helps a classifier and then hurts it, because the data become sparse in a space of growing volume and the model fits noise in irrelevant features — Hughes showed in 1968 that accuracy peaks at an optimal number of features and then declines.[9] How many features help is answered on held-out data (Section 11); the screen of Section 2.4 is the crudest form. Association analysis searches transactional data — purchases, prescriptions, co-occurring diagnoses — for IF–THEN rules ("patients prescribed A and B are also prescribed C") with sufficient support and confidence; the Apriori algorithm is the classical method,[10] and its rules are the data-mining counterpart of expert-system rules, discovered rather than written. Without labels the performance measure is ambiguous — how good is a clustering? — the paradigm's central difficulty, and also what makes it cheap.

3.4 Reinforcement learning

The experience is generated by the learner's actions: an agent observes a state, chooses an action, receives a scalar reward and a new state; the task is a policy — states to actions — maximising cumulative reward. The feedback is evaluative (how good the action was, not what the right one was) and delayed, hence the credit-assignment problem of attributing outcomes to earlier actions. Sutton and Barto's textbook is the reference.[11] AlphaGo was reinforcement learning; in medicine it has been used, controversially, to propose fluid and vasopressor dosing in sepsis.[12] Section 10.2 implements the two basic algorithms.

3.5 Modern additions: semi-supervised and self-supervised learning

Semi-supervised learning uses a small labelled set with a large unlabelled one: the unlabelled data cannot name the classes, but a boundary through a sparse region is more plausible than one cutting a dense cluster.[13] Self-supervised learning manufactures labels from the data — hide part of an input (the next word, a masked image patch) and predict it — then fine-tunes the learned representation on a small labelled set; it is how language models are pre-trained and increasingly how medical imaging models are built when labels are scarce.[14]

Key idea

Paradigms are distinguished by the feedback in $E$, not by the algorithm. The same network can be trained supervised, self-supervised or by reinforcement. "Uses deep learning" names the model family; it does not yet say what the model learned from.

Bridge to bioinformatics

A QSAR model is supervised regression; hierarchical clustering of an expression matrix is unsupervised; protein language models such as ESM are self-supervised, trained to predict masked residues from context.

4. Approaches to pattern recognition

Unit 1 (Section 3) distinguished symbolic, connectionist, statistical and evolutionary approaches to AI. Pattern recognition inherits the last three; the classical review of the field names the statistical and neural approaches, and the course plan adds the evolutionary one.[15]

Approach How the decision rule is obtained Methods Units
Statistical Model the classes, or the posterior probability of the class given the features, and estimate parameters from the sample Bayes classifiers, discriminant analysis, logistic regression, k-NN, trees, SVM 2–5
Neural Connect simple units with adjustable weights; adjust them iteratively to reduce training error[16] Perceptron, multi-layer and convolutional networks 6, 8
Evolutionary Keep a population of candidate rules; score, select, recombine, mutate, repeat[17] Genetic algorithms, evolution strategies 7

Historically different disciplines, in practice they are three ways of searching for the same thing. The cell separates malignant from benign aspirates with the two features of Unit 1 using one representative of each: linear discriminant analysis computes a line in closed form from class means and a pooled covariance; the perceptron starts from a random line and nudges it after each misclassified case; an evolution strategy keeps 20 random lines, scores them by accuracy and breeds the best five with mutation for 40 generations.

# One problem, three approaches: statistical (LDA), neural (perceptron), evolutionary (evolution strategy).
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.linear_model import Perceptron

X2 = X[["mean radius", "mean concave points"]].to_numpy() * np.array([1, 100])   # as in Unit 1
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X2); yv = y.to_numpy()

lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(Xs, yv)                        # statistical: closed form
per = Perceptron(random_state=0).fit(Xs, yv)                           # neural: error-driven updates

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)                                         # evolutionary: (5 + 15) evolution strategy
def accuracy(w):
    '''Accuracy of the linear rule "benign if w0*x1 + w1*x2 + w2 > 0".'''
    return (((Xs @ w[:2] + w[2]) > 0).astype(int) == yv).mean()
pop = rng.normal(size=(20, 3)); history = []
for gen in range(40):
    fit = np.array([accuracy(w) for w in pop]); parents = pop[np.argsort(-fit)[:5]]; history.append(fit.max())
    children = parents[rng.integers(0, 5, 15)] + rng.normal(0, 0.3, (15, 3))
    pop = np.vstack([parents, children])
w_es = pop[np.argmax([accuracy(w) for w in pop])]

print(f"training accuracy  LDA {lda.score(Xs, yv):.3f} | perceptron {per.score(Xs, yv):.3f} (after {per.n_iter_} passes) "
      f"| evolution strategy {accuracy(w_es):.3f} (generation 1: {history[0]:.3f})")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.5, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
for c, col, name in [(0, ORANGE, "malignant"), (1, BLUE, "benign")]:
    ax.scatter(*Xs[yv == c].T, color=col, s=9, alpha=0.6, label=name)
xx = np.linspace(-2.5, 4, 50)
for (w, b), lab, ls in [((lda.coef_[0], lda.intercept_[0]), "statistical (LDA)", "-"),
                        ((per.coef_[0], per.intercept_[0]), "neural (perceptron)", "--"),
                        ((w_es[:2], w_es[2]), "evolutionary (ES)", ":")]:
    ax.plot(xx, -(w[0] * xx + b) / w[1], ls, color="k", lw=1.3, label=lab)
ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 5); ax.set_xlabel("mean radius (standardised)"); ax.set_ylabel("mean concave points (standardised)")
ax.legend(fontsize=7.5, frameon=False); ax.set_title("Three approaches, one straight boundary")
axes[1].plot(range(1, 41), history, color=GREEN); axes[1].set_xlabel("generation"); axes[1].set_ylabel("best accuracy in population")
axes[1].set_title("Evolution strategy: fitness of the best rule"); fig.tight_layout()

training accuracy  LDA 0.910 | perceptron 0.916 (after 8 passes) | evolution strategy 0.928 (generation 1: 0.907)

Figure 3. Left: the 569 aspirates in the standardised feature space and the boundaries found by a statistical (solid), a neural (dashed) and an evolutionary (dotted) method. All three are straight lines through the zone of overlap with training accuracies between 0.91 and 0.93; their slopes differ because each optimises a different criterion and the data do not single out one line. Right: the best accuracy in the evolutionary population plateaus after a few generations. LDA needed one computation, the perceptron 8 passes, the evolution strategy 800 evaluations.

The hypothesis space is the same — straight lines — so none can beat the best line; the approaches differ in how they search and in what else they offer: probabilities (statistical), scale to millions of parameters (neural), optimisation without gradients (evolutionary; Section 7 explains why that matters). Modern practice mixes them freely.

Exercise 1

Change the mutation scale in the evolution strategy from 0.3 to 0.03 and to 3.0. Small mutations improve slowly; large ones never settle. This is the learning-rate trade-off of Section 7 and the mutation rate of Unit 7.

5. What a classifier is

5.1 Definition and decision boundary

A classifier is a function $\hat{y} = f(\mathbf{x})$ from feature vectors to a finite set of labels $\{1, \dots, K\}$. Because labels are finite and feature space is continuous, every classifier partitions the space into $K$ decision regions separated by decision boundaries; everything it "knows" is where those boundaries lie. Most useful classifiers output a score per class — best of all a probability $P(y = k \mid \mathbf{x})$ — and a decision rule turns scores into a label. The separation matters because the decision rule is where the costs of errors enter: a missed malignancy costs far more than an unnecessary biopsy, and "malignant if $P > 0.5$" is almost never the right rule (Section 9.5).

5.2 The catalogue of the course

The plan lists Bayesian networks, decision trees, k-means, neural networks and genetic algorithms. The cell trains a representative of four families on the same two features and draws their regions; the fifth, k-means, is treated in Section 10 for the reason in the box below.

# Four families of classifiers on the same two features: the shapes of their decision regions.
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X2, yv, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=yv)
models = {
    "Bayesian (Gaussian naive Bayes) — Unit 3": GaussianNB(),
    "k-nearest neighbours (k = 15) — Unit 3":   KNeighborsClassifier(15),
    "Decision tree (depth 3) — Unit 4":          DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0),
    "Neural network (2 x 8 units) — Unit 6":    MLPClassifier((8, 8), max_iter=3000, random_state=0),
}
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(6, 30, 200), np.linspace(-1, 22, 200)); grid = np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(9.5, 2.7), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, m) in zip(axes, models.items()):
    m.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    ax.contourf(xx, yy, m.predict(grid).reshape(xx.shape), levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5], colors=["#fbe3d3", "#dfe7f1"])
    for c, col in [(0, ORANGE), (1, BLUE)]:
        ax.scatter(*X_te[y_te == c].T, color=col, s=6, edgecolor="none")
    ax.set_title(name.split(" — ")[0] + f"\ntest accuracy {m.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel("mean radius"); ax.text(7, 20, name.split(" — ")[1], fontsize=7, color=GREY)
axes[0].set_ylabel("mean concave points x 100"); fig.tight_layout()

Figure 4. Decision regions (orange malignant, blue benign) of four families trained on the same 398 cases and evaluated on the same 171 held-out cases (dots). Naive Bayes gives a smooth curve from two Gaussians per class; k-nearest neighbours an irregular boundary following the local majority; the tree axis-parallel rectangles, each decision comparing one feature with one threshold; the network a smooth curve of free shape. Test accuracies lie between 0.89 and 0.91 — no family is decisively better, a finding documented across many benchmarks.[18] The differences that matter are interpretability, cost, data requirements and robustness.

A correction to the plan: k-means is not a classifier

The plan lists k-means among "classification techniques". k-means is a clustering algorithm: it partitions unlabelled data into $k$ groups by minimising within-group variance and never sees or predicts a class label.[19][20] Its output looks like a classification and it shares a letter with k-nearest neighbours, but the two have nothing else in common. Accepted statement: k-means is the canonical unsupervised method (Unit 5, Section 10.1); k-nearest neighbours is a supervised classifier (Unit 3, Figure 4). Likewise "Bayesian networks" are a general formalism of which the Bayesian classifiers of Unit 3 are the special case the course develops, and "genetic algorithms" are an optimisation method (Section 4, Unit 7) that can build classifiers but is not one.

What the rest of this unit does

Figure 4 shows what classifiers produce; nothing so far shows how their parameters are found, which is what learning means. Sections 6–9 answer that for the simplest models — a straight line for a number, a straight line for a probability — in complete detail. Every later unit is a variation on the same three steps.

6. Linear regression: the first learning problem

The dataset for Sections 6–8: 442 patients with diabetes, ten baseline variables — age, sex, body-mass index, blood pressure and six serum measurements — and a quantitative measure of disease progression one year later as the target,[21] loaded in original units.

# The diabetes dataset in its original units: 442 patients x 10 baseline variables, and the target
# (a quantitative measure of disease progression one year after baseline).
diab = datasets.load_diabetes(as_frame=True, scaled=False)
Xd, yd = diab.data, diab.target
print("X shape:", Xd.shape, "| target: mean %.1f, sd %.1f, range %d-%d" % (yd.mean(), yd.std(), yd.min(), yd.max()))
desc = Xd.describe().T[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(1)
desc["meaning"] = ["age (years)", "sex (1/2)", "body-mass index", "mean arterial pressure", "total cholesterol (tc)",
                   "LDL cholesterol", "HDL cholesterol", "tc/HDL ratio", "log serum triglycerides", "blood glucose"]
desc

Ten variables on very different scales — BMI 18–42, total cholesterol 97–301 — which matters in Section 7. The target has mean 152 and standard deviation 77: a predictor that always outputs the mean errs by 77 typically, and any model must do better.

6.1 The model

Regression is supervised learning with a numerical target. The simplest model makes the target a linear function of the features plus noise:

$$\hat{y} = f_{\boldsymbol\beta}(\mathbf{x}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p = \mathbf{x}^\top \boldsymbol\beta$$ where the second form absorbs the intercept by prepending a constant feature $x_0 = 1$, so that $\mathbf{x}$ and $\boldsymbol\beta$ have length $p + 1$.

The hypothesis space is the set of hyperplanes, the parameters the $p + 1$ coefficients. The name is Galton's 1886 "regression towards mediocrity" of children's heights, which stuck to the method he used — fitting a line.[22]

6.2 The loss: least squares

The classical measure of fit is the sum of squared residuals, $r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$ being the vertical distance from observation to line:

$$L(\boldsymbol\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol\beta\right)^2 = \lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2$$ where $\mathbf{X}$ is the $n \times (p+1)$ data matrix with a leading column of ones. Divided by $n$ it is the mean squared error (MSE), with the same minimiser; its square root (RMSE) is in the units of $y$.

Why squares? They are differentiable, so the minimum has a closed form; they penalise a few large errors more than many small ones; and under Gaussian noise minimising squared error is maximising the likelihood of the data — the principle behind every loss in this course, used in Section 9 for logistic regression. Legendre published the method in 1805, Gauss claimed it from 1795, and the dispute is one of the best documented in the history of science.[23]

6.3 Worked example by hand: four points

Four patients with body-mass index $x$ and progression score $y$ (invented round values):

patient $x$ (BMI) $y$ (progression)
1 20 100
2 24 120
3 28 180
4 32 200

For one feature the least-squares line $\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ has the textbook solution (a special case of Section 6.4):

$$\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \qquad \beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1 \bar{x}.$$

Step 1 — means. $\bar{x} = (20 + 24 + 28 + 32)/4 = 26$; $\bar{y} = (100 + 120 + 180 + 200)/4 = 150$.

Step 2 — deviations.

$i$ $x_i - \bar{x}$ $y_i - \bar{y}$ product $(x_i - \bar{x})^2$
1 −6 −50 300 36
2 −2 −30 60 4
3 2 30 60 4
4 6 50 300 36
sum 720 80

Step 3 — coefficients. $\beta_1 = 720/80 = 9$ progression units per BMI unit; $\beta_0 = 150 - 9 \times 26 = -84$.

Step 4 — check. Predictions $(96, 132, 168, 204)$; residuals $(4, -12, 12, -4)$, summing to zero as least-squares residuals always do with an intercept; squared sum $320$, MSE $80$. The cell confirms the arithmetic and that no other slope does better.

# The four-point example: the hand-computed line, and a check that nearby lines have a larger loss.
x4 = np.array([20., 24., 28., 32.]); y4 = np.array([100., 120., 180., 200.])
b1 = ((x4 - x4.mean()) * (y4 - y4.mean())).sum() / ((x4 - x4.mean()) ** 2).sum()
b0 = y4.mean() - b1 * x4.mean()
resid = y4 - (b0 + b1 * x4)
print(f"slope = {b1:.1f}, intercept = {b0:.1f}, residuals = {resid}, sum = {resid.sum():.1f}, MSE = {(resid**2).mean():.1f}")

def mse(b0_, b1_): return ((y4 - (b0_ + b1_ * x4)) ** 2).mean()
print("MSE of the hand-computed line        :", mse(b0, b1))
print("MSE with the slope changed to 8 or 10:", mse(y4.mean() - 8 * x4.mean(), 8), mse(y4.mean() - 10 * x4.mean(), 10))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.3))
xx = np.linspace(18, 34, 10)
axes[0].scatter(x4, y4, color=BLUE, s=50, zorder=3, label="four patients")
axes[0].plot(xx, b0 + b1 * xx, color=ORANGE, label=f"least-squares line  y = {b0:.0f} + {b1:.0f} x")
for xi, yi, ri in zip(x4, y4, resid):
    axes[0].plot([xi, xi], [yi, yi - ri], color=GREY, lw=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("body-mass index"); axes[0].set_ylabel("progression score"); axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_title("The fitted line and its residuals (grey)")
slopes = np.linspace(4, 14, 100)
axes[1].plot(slopes, [mse(y4.mean() - s * x4.mean(), s) for s in slopes], color=BLUE)
axes[1].plot(b1, mse(b0, b1), "o", color=ORANGE, ms=8); axes[1].set_xlabel("slope (with the intercept chosen optimally for each slope)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("mean squared error"); axes[1].set_title("The loss is a parabola in the slope; its minimum is at 9")
fig.tight_layout()

slope = 9.0, intercept = -84.0, residuals = [  4. -12.  12.  -4.], sum = 0.0, MSE = 80.0
MSE of the hand-computed line        : 80.0
MSE with the slope changed to 8 or 10: 100.0 100.0

Figure 5. Left: the four patients, the line $\hat{y} = -84 + 9x$ and the residuals (grey), whose squares the method minimises. Right: the MSE as a function of the slope, with the intercept re-optimised for each slope — a parabola with a unique minimum at slope 9 and MSE 80. With one minimum, any downhill method finds it; logistic regression shares this property.

6.4 The normal equations

Expand the loss in matrix form:

$$L(\boldsymbol\beta) = (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta)^\top (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta) = \mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{y} - 2\,\boldsymbol\beta^\top \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y} + \boldsymbol\beta^\top \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\, \boldsymbol\beta.$$

A bowl in $p + 1$ dimensions; at the minimum the gradient is zero. With $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\, \mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{a}$ and $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\, \boldsymbol\beta^\top \mathbf{A} \boldsymbol\beta = 2\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol\beta$:

$$\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta} L = -2\,\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y} + 2\,\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\,\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\;\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\, \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y}\;} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y}.$$

These are the normal equations: $p + 1$ linear equations in $p + 1$ unknowns, uniquely solvable when no feature is an exact linear combination of the others and $n > p$. The name is geometric: the residual vector is normal to every column of $\mathbf{X}$, so the fitted values are the projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the feature space. For one feature they reduce to the hand formulas (Exercise 2). In code one never forms the inverse: np.linalg.solve solves the system directly, and scikit-learn's LinearRegression uses a singular-value decomposition.

# Normal equations with one feature (BMI) on the 442 diabetes patients, checked against scikit-learn.
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
x_bmi = Xd["bmi"].to_numpy(); y_prog = yd.to_numpy()
X1 = np.c_[np.ones(len(x_bmi)), x_bmi]                      # n x 2 design matrix: column of ones, then BMI
beta1 = np.linalg.solve(X1.T @ X1, X1.T @ y_prog)             # solve (X'X) beta = X'y
yhat1 = X1 @ beta1
rss, tss = ((y_prog - yhat1) ** 2).sum(), ((y_prog - y_prog.mean()) ** 2).sum()
print(f"X'X =\n{(X1.T @ X1).round(0)}\nX'y = {(X1.T @ y_prog).round(0)}")
print(f"beta (intercept, slope) = {beta1.round(3)}  |  RMSE = {np.sqrt(rss / len(y_prog)):.1f}  |  R^2 = {1 - rss / tss:.3f}")
sk = LinearRegression().fit(x_bmi[:, None], y_prog)
print(f"scikit-learn: intercept = {sk.intercept_:.3f}, slope = {sk.coef_[0]:.3f}  (identical)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
ax.scatter(x_bmi, y_prog, s=10, color=BLUE, alpha=0.5, label="442 patients")
xx = np.linspace(17, 43, 10); ax.plot(xx, beta1[0] + beta1[1] * xx, color=ORANGE, lw=2, label=f"y = {beta1[0]:.0f} + {beta1[1]:.1f} x")
ax.set_xlabel("body-mass index at baseline"); ax.set_ylabel("disease progression after one year"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_title("Least-squares line: progression against BMI"); fig.tight_layout()

X'X =
[[   442.  11658.]
 [ 11658. 316100.]]
X'y = [  67243. 1861677.]
beta (intercept, slope) = [-117.773   10.233]  |  RMSE = 62.4  |  R^2 = 0.344
scikit-learn: intercept = -117.773, slope = 10.233  (identical)

Figure 6. Progression against BMI for 442 patients and the least-squares line, slope about 10.2: each additional BMI unit is associated with about ten more units of progression on average. The scatter is wide — RMSE about 62 against the 77 of the do-nothing predictor — so BMI alone explains a modest fraction of the variation.

6.5 Reading the output: coefficients and R²

A coefficient says how the prediction changes with its feature: two patients differing by one BMI unit are predicted to differ by 10.2 progression units, all else held equal — vacuous with one feature, essential with ten. The intercept (prediction at BMI 0) is meaningless here; centring the feature (Section 7) makes it the mean of $y$. The coefficient of determination

$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2} = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}}$$ compares the model's residual sum of squares with that of the do-nothing predictor $\hat{y} = \bar{y}$: 1 means every point on the line, 0 no better than the mean; on training data it cannot be negative when an intercept is fitted, on new data it can.

With BMI alone $R^2 \approx 0.34$ — a third of the variance "explained" statistically, which implies nothing about causation. With ten features only the width of $\mathbf{X}$ changes.

# Normal equations with all ten features. The code is the same; only the design matrix is wider.
X10 = np.c_[np.ones(len(y_prog)), Xd.to_numpy()]                # n x 11
beta10 = np.linalg.solve(X10.T @ X10, X10.T @ y_prog)
yhat10 = X10 @ beta10
r2_10 = 1 - ((y_prog - yhat10) ** 2).sum() / tss
print(f"R^2 with ten features = {r2_10:.3f}  (BMI alone: {1 - rss / tss:.3f})  |  RMSE = {np.sqrt(((y_prog - yhat10) ** 2).mean()):.1f}")

# Coefficients in original units and, for comparability, per standard deviation of each feature.
coef = pd.DataFrame({"coefficient (per unit)": beta10[1:], "feature sd": Xd.std().to_numpy()}, index=Xd.columns)
coef["effect of +1 sd"] = coef["coefficient (per unit)"] * coef["feature sd"]
coef.round(2).sort_values("effect of +1 sd", key=abs, ascending=False)

s5 68.48 0.52 35.77

$R^2$ rises to 0.52 and the RMSE falls to 54. The BMI coefficient drops from 10.2 to 5.6: part of what BMI "explained" alone is now attributed to variables it correlates with. Raw coefficients are not comparable — triglycerides (68) look large only because that variable is on a log scale with standard deviation 0.5 — so the third column rescales each per standard deviation of its feature: triglycerides, BMI, LDL and blood pressure contribute most positively, total cholesterol most negatively, and age almost nothing once the others are known. This reading of coefficients is the basis of every multivariable risk model in medicine.

Two cautions

A coefficient describes how the prediction changes, not what would happen to the patient if the feature changed. And when features are strongly correlated — total cholesterol, LDL and the tc/HDL ratio — $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is nearly singular and coefficients become unstable: large, of opposite signs, sensitive to a few patients, while predictions stay fine. The pair s1 = −38 and s2 = +23 per standard deviation is this instability. Ridge regression (Section 8.3) was invented for it.[24]

6.6 Residual plots

$R^2$ hides where the model fails; residuals show it. Against fitted values they should form a structureless band — a curve means non-linearity, a funnel noise growing with the prediction (heteroscedasticity); their histogram should be roughly symmetric.

# Residual diagnostics for the ten-feature model.
resid10 = y_prog - yhat10
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.4))
axes[0].scatter(yhat10, resid10, s=10, color=BLUE, alpha=0.5); axes[0].axhline(0, color="k", lw=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("fitted value"); axes[0].set_ylabel("residual (observed - fitted)"); axes[0].set_title("Residuals against fitted values")
axes[1].hist(resid10, bins=30, color=BLUE, alpha=0.7); axes[1].axvline(0, color="k", lw=1)
axes[1].set_xlabel("residual"); axes[1].set_ylabel("patients"); axes[1].set_title("Distribution of residuals")
fig.tight_layout()
print(f"residual mean = {resid10.mean():.2e} (zero by construction) | sd = {resid10.std():.1f} | "
      f"skewness = {scipy.stats.skew(resid10):.2f} | largest |residual| = {np.abs(resid10).max():.0f}")

residual mean = 1.02e-13 (zero by construction) | sd = 53.5 | skewness = 0.02 | largest |residual| = 156

Figure 7. Left: residuals of the ten-feature model against fitted values. The band is roughly horizontal, so a linear model is not grossly wrong; the diagonal lower edge at the left is a floor effect (scores cannot fall below 25) that Gaussian noise cannot represent. Right: residuals nearly symmetric (skewness 0.02), standard deviation 54. Acceptable for a first model; the next step would be a transformed target or a non-linear model (Unit 4).

Exercise 2

(a) Verify on paper that for one feature with an intercept the normal equations are $n\beta_0 + \beta_1 \sum x_i = \sum y_i$ and $\beta_0 \sum x_i + \beta_1 \sum x_i^2 = \sum x_i y_i$, and that solving them gives the formulas of Section 6.3. (b) Remove the columns s1 and s2 from the ten-feature cell and re-fit. How much do $R^2$ and the remaining coefficients change?

7. Gradient descent: how a machine learns

7.1 Why a closed form is not enough

Almost no learning problem has a closed form: logistic regression (Section 9) has none, a neural network's loss surface has no formula for its minimum, and even linear regression with $p$ in the hundreds of thousands cannot form $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$. What every problem has is a loss that can be evaluated and differentiated. Gradient descent uses nothing else, trains essentially every modern model, and is the moment at which "the machine learns" stops being a metaphor.

7.2 The idea

The gradient $\nabla L(\theta)$ is the vector of partial derivatives; it points uphill, so its negative points downhill. Start anywhere and repeat

$$\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta\, \nabla L(\theta^{(t)})$$ where $\eta > 0$ is the learning rate; stop when the gradient is nearly zero, when the loss stops changing, or after a fixed number of steps.

The learning rate has three regimes: too small, correct but slow; too large, each step overshoots and the loss diverges; in between, fast convergence. For a quadratic loss the boundary is exact — $\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}$, the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian — and the speed is set by the ratio of largest to smallest eigenvalue, the condition number, large when features have different scales. Hence feature scaling, optional for the normal equations, is almost mandatory for gradient descent.

7.3 The gradient of the least-squares loss

For the MSE $L(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2$, Section 6.4 gives

$$\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta} L = -\frac{2}{n}\, \mathbf{X}^\top (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta) = -\frac{2}{n}\, \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{r},$$

the correlation of each feature with the residuals: if a feature is high where the model under-predicts, its coefficient goes up. The cell implements the three-line update for the BMI problem with the feature centred (intercept = mean of $y$, parameters uncorrelated) at three learning rates.

# Batch gradient descent for least squares, by hand. Three learning rates: too small, good, too large.
xc = x_bmi - x_bmi.mean()                               # centred BMI: intercept becomes the mean of y
Xc = np.c_[np.ones(len(xc)), xc]
beta_closed = np.linalg.solve(Xc.T @ Xc, Xc.T @ y_prog)  # closed form for comparison

def gradient_descent(X_, y_, lr, steps=100):
    '''Batch gradient descent on the mean squared error. Returns the parameter path and the loss per step.'''
    beta = np.zeros(X_.shape[1]); path, losses = [beta.copy()], []
    for t in range(steps):
        r = y_ - X_ @ beta                              # residuals with the current parameters
        losses.append((r ** 2).mean())                  # loss before the step
        grad = -2 / len(y_) * X_.T @ r                  # gradient of the MSE
        beta = beta - lr * grad                         # the learning step
        path.append(beta.copy())
    return np.array(path), np.array(losses)

lam_max = 2 * np.linalg.eigvalsh(Xc.T @ Xc / len(y_prog)).max()
print(f"largest Hessian eigenvalue = {lam_max:.1f}  ->  gradient descent converges only if lr < 2/{lam_max:.1f} = {2 / lam_max:.4f}")
runs = {lr: gradient_descent(Xc, y_prog, lr) for lr in [0.005, 0.04, 0.055]}
for lr, (path, losses) in runs.items():
    print(f"lr = {lr:<6}  after 100 steps: beta = {path[-1].round(2)}   MSE = {losses[-1]:.4g}")
print(f"closed form:               beta = {beta_closed.round(2)}   MSE = {((y_prog - Xc @ beta_closed) ** 2).mean():.4g}")

largest Hessian eigenvalue = 39.0  ->  gradient descent converges only if lr < 2/39.0 = 0.0513
lr = 0.005   after 100 steps: beta = [96.45 10.23]   MSE = 7054
lr = 0.04    after 100 steps: beta = [152.1   10.23]   MSE = 3890
lr = 0.055   after 100 steps: beta = [ 1.52130000e+02 -6.14869428e+06]   MSE = 5.643e+14
closed form:               beta = [152.13  10.23]   MSE = 3890

The three regimes appear. At $\eta = 0.005$ the loss is still falling after 100 steps and the intercept (96) is far from 152, while the slope — the direction of larger curvature — converged long ago. At $\eta = 0.04$ both parameters match the closed form and the MSE equals the minimum, 3890. At $\eta = 0.055$, just above the threshold of 0.051, the slope oscillates with growing amplitude and the loss reaches $10^{14}$.

# Convergence curves for the three learning rates, and the path of the good one on the loss surface.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
for (lr, (path, losses)), col in zip(runs.items(), [GREY, BLUE, ORANGE]):
    axes[0].plot(np.clip(losses, 1, 1e6), color=col, label=f"lr = {lr}" + ("  (diverges)" if losses[-1] > 1e6 else ""))
axes[0].axhline(((y_prog - Xc @ beta_closed) ** 2).mean(), color="k", ls="--", lw=1, label="closed-form minimum")
axes[0].set_yscale("log"); axes[0].set_xlabel("step"); axes[0].set_ylabel("mean squared error (log scale, clipped)")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); axes[0].set_title("Loss per step for three learning rates")

# Loss surface in the (intercept, slope) plane and the path for lr = 0.04 and lr = 0.005
b0g, b1g = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-20, 320, 120), np.linspace(-30, 50, 120))
L = np.array([[((y_prog - (a + b * xc)) ** 2).mean() for a in b0g[0]] for b in b1g[:, 0]])
cs = axes[1].contour(b0g, b1g, L, levels=np.geomspace(4000, 60000, 12), colors=GREY, linewidths=0.6)
for lr, col in [(0.005, GREY), (0.04, BLUE)]:
    p = runs[lr][0]; axes[1].plot(p[:, 0], p[:, 1], "o-", color=col, ms=2.5, lw=1, label=f"path, lr = {lr}")
axes[1].plot(*beta_closed, "*", color=ORANGE, ms=14, label="closed-form solution")
axes[1].set_xlabel("intercept"); axes[1].set_ylabel("slope"); axes[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
axes[1].set_title("Descent on the loss surface (contours of the MSE)"); fig.tight_layout()

Figure 8. Left: MSE per step for the three rates (log axis). The small rate descends steadily but has not reached the minimum (dashed) after 100 steps; the moderate rate reaches it in a few dozen; the large rate decreases briefly and then grows without bound (clipped at $10^6$). Right: the loss surface over (intercept, slope). The contours are elongated because the slope direction is curved about twenty times more sharply than the intercept direction; the moderate-rate path zig-zags down the steep direction and then creeps along the flat one. This is the condition number made visible; standardising the feature would make the contours circles.

This is what learning is

Nothing in the gradient-descent cell knows about diabetes or lines; it knows a loss and its gradient and walks downhill. Replace the model by a network with a million weights and the loss by that of Section 9, keep the three lines of the update, and you have the training loop of every deep-learning system.

7.4 Stochastic gradient descent

The gradient above used all $n$ patients at every step — batch descent. With a million images that is unnecessary: a gradient from a random mini-batch is a noisy but unbiased estimate of the full one. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) does this with a decreasing learning rate so the noise averages out; the convergence proof is Robbins and Monro's 1951 stochastic approximation.[25] The cell runs scikit-learn's SGD on the ten-feature problem with and without scaling.

# Stochastic gradient descent in scikit-learn on the ten-feature problem, with and without feature scaling.
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDRegressor
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")              # SGD on raw features emits convergence warnings

sgd_raw    = SGDRegressor(max_iter=1000, random_state=0, learning_rate="invscaling", eta0=1e-4).fit(Xd, y_prog)
sgd_scaled = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SGDRegressor(max_iter=1000, random_state=0)).fit(Xd, y_prog)
ols        = LinearRegression().fit(Xd, y_prog)
res = pd.DataFrame({
    "R^2 (training)": [ols.score(Xd, y_prog), sgd_raw.score(Xd, y_prog), sgd_scaled.score(Xd, y_prog)],
    "passes over the data": ["1 (closed form)", sgd_raw.n_iter_, sgd_scaled[-1].n_iter_],
}, index=["normal equations", "SGD on raw features", "SGD on standardised features"])
res["R^2 (training)"] = res["R^2 (training)"].map(lambda v: f"{v:.3f}" if abs(v) < 10 else f"{v:.1e}  (diverged)")
res
R^2 (training) passes over the data
normal equations 0.518 1 (closed form)
SGD on raw features -8.3e+10  (diverged) 114
SGD on standardised features 0.514 14

On standardised features SGD reaches the $R^2$ of the normal equations (0.51 against 0.52) in 14 passes. On raw features — cholesterol in the hundreds, log-triglycerides near 4.6 — it diverges to an $R^2$ of order $-10^{10}$: no single rate suits all directions of so elongated a surface. Standardise before any gradient-based method.

Exercise 3

Replace the centred feature xc by the standardised one (x_bmi - x_bmi.mean()) / x_bmi.std() and re-run both cells: the threshold becomes lr < 1 and the contours circles. Find a rate that reaches the minimum in fewer than ten steps. Then run steps=1000 with lr=0.005 on the centred feature and confirm that the small rate gets there in the end.

8. Overfitting: a preview

8.1 More flexible is not better

The linear model is often wrong: dose–response curves saturate, signals oscillate. Polynomial regression replaces $x$ by $x, x^2, \dots, x^d$ and fits a linear model to them — linear in the parameters, so the normal equations apply unchanged, but the curve can bend, and the degree $d$ controls flexibility. The experiment draws 20 training points from a sine curve plus noise, fits degrees 1, 3 and 15, and evaluates each on the training points and on 200 new points from the same curve.

# Polynomial regression on a synthetic 1-D problem: training error versus error on new data.
from numpy.polynomial import Polynomial
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
truth = lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)
xp_tr = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 1, 20)); yp_tr = truth(xp_tr) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, 20)        # 20 noisy training points
rng2 = np.random.default_rng(1)
xp_te = np.sort(rng2.uniform(xp_tr.min(), xp_tr.max(), 200)); yp_te = truth(xp_te) + rng2.normal(0, 0.3, 200)  # 200 new points
xx = np.linspace(xp_tr.min(), xp_tr.max(), 400)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.5, 3.0), sharey=True); rows = []
for ax, d in zip(axes, [1, 3, 15]):
    P = Polynomial.fit(xp_tr, yp_tr, d)                      # least squares on a well-conditioned basis
    tr, te = ((P(xp_tr) - yp_tr) ** 2).mean(), ((P(xp_te) - yp_te) ** 2).mean()
    rows.append(dict(degree=d, parameters=d + 1, train_MSE=tr, test_MSE=te))
    ax.plot(xx, truth(xx), color=GREY, lw=1, ls="--", label="true curve")
    ax.scatter(xp_tr, yp_tr, color=BLUE, s=22, zorder=3, label="training points")
    ax.plot(xx, P(xx), color=ORANGE, lw=1.8, label=f"degree-{d} fit")
    ax.set_ylim(-2, 2); ax.set_title(f"degree {d}: train MSE {tr:.3f}, test MSE {te:.3f}", fontsize=8.5); ax.set_xlabel("x")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7.5); fig.tight_layout()
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)
degree parameters train_MSE test_MSE
0 1 2 0.231 0.287
1 3 4 0.026 0.090
2 15 16 0.003 1.953

Figure 9. Three polynomial fits (orange) to 20 noisy points (blue) from a sine curve (dashed). Degree 1 cannot follow the curve and errs equally on training and test points: it underfits. Degree 3 follows the curve with the lowest test error, 0.090 — essentially the noise variance $0.3^2 = 0.09$, the best any model could do. Degree 15 passes almost through the training points (training MSE 0.003) but swings wildly between them; its test error, 1.95, is more than twenty times the cubic's: it overfits, having learned the noise of the sample rather than the pattern.

8.2 Training error is not the quantity of interest

The table states the most important methodological lesson of the course: training error decreases monotonically with flexibility and is useless for choosing the model. What matters is the generalisation error on unseen data, which falls, reaches a minimum at the right flexibility and rises again. Supplement S1 develops the methodology; here the point is to recognise the phenomenon, because every classifier in Figure 4 has a flexibility knob — tree depth, neighbours, network size — and every one can overfit.

8.3 Regularisation: ridge regression

Degree 15 is under-constrained: nothing stops the coefficients growing to absurd values to thread the noise. Regularisation adds a penalty on coefficient size to the loss, trading fit against simplicity. Ridge regression (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970)[24] is the oldest form:

$$L_{\text{ridge}}(\boldsymbol\beta) = \lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2 + \lambda \lVert \boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{ridge}} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y}$$ where $\lambda \ge 0$ (scikit-learn's alpha) sets the strength and the intercept is left unpenalised by centring $\mathbf{y}$ and the features. The solution is the normal equations with $\lambda$ on the diagonal — the "ridge" — which makes the matrix invertible even when $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is singular and shrinks all coefficients towards zero.

The cell applies this formula to the degree-15 features, standardised so the penalty treats all powers equally.

# Ridge regression on the degree-15 features: the normal equations with lambda on the diagonal.
def poly_design(xv, d, lo, hi):
    '''Powers 1..d of x mapped to [-1, 1] (no intercept column; the intercept is the mean of y).'''
    t = 2 * (xv - lo) / (hi - lo) - 1
    return np.vander(t, d + 1, increasing=True)[:, 1:]
lo, hi = xp_tr.min(), xp_tr.max()
Phi = poly_design(xp_tr, 15, lo, hi); mu, sd = Phi.mean(0), Phi.std(0)
Phi_tr, Phi_te, Phi_xx = (Phi - mu) / sd, (poly_design(xp_te, 15, lo, hi) - mu) / sd, (poly_design(xx, 15, lo, hi) - mu) / sd

rows, curves = [], {}
for lam in [0, 1e-4, 1e-2, 1, 100]:
    b = np.linalg.solve(Phi_tr.T @ Phi_tr + lam * np.eye(15), Phi_tr.T @ (yp_tr - yp_tr.mean()))   # ridge normal equations
    pred = lambda P: P @ b + yp_tr.mean()
    rows.append(dict(**{"lambda": lam}, train_MSE=((pred(Phi_tr) - yp_tr) ** 2).mean(), test_MSE=((pred(Phi_te) - yp_te) ** 2).mean(),
                     coef_norm=np.linalg.norm(b)))
    curves[lam] = pred(Phi_xx)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.4))
ax.plot(xx, truth(xx), color=GREY, ls="--", lw=1, label="true curve"); ax.scatter(xp_tr, yp_tr, color=BLUE, s=22, zorder=3, label="training points")
for lam, col in [(0, ORANGE), (1e-2, GREEN), (100, "k")]:
    ax.plot(xx, curves[lam], color=col, lw=1.6, label=f"degree 15, lambda = {lam:g}")
ax.set_ylim(-2, 2); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, ncol=2); ax.set_title("Ridge regularisation tames the degree-15 polynomial"); fig.tight_layout()
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4)
lambda train_MSE test_MSE coef_norm
0 0.0000 0.0032 1.9528 15372.8556
1 0.0001 0.0125 0.1014 21.0543
2 0.0100 0.0205 0.1043 2.0972
3 1.0000 0.0569 0.1388 1.0176
4 100.0000 0.3669 0.5584 0.0823

Figure 10. The degree-15 polynomial under three penalties. $\lambda = 0$ (orange) is the fit of Figure 9, coefficient norm about 15,000. $\lambda = 0.01$ (green): the same sixteen parameters give a smooth curve tracking the truth as well as the cubic — test MSE 0.10, coefficient norm 2.1, four orders of magnitude smaller. $\lambda = 100$ (black): the penalty dominates and the curve underfits. Regularisation strength is a second flexibility knob, chosen like the degree on held-out data (Supplement S1).

Bridge to later units and to QSAR

Every model has such a knob: C in logistic regression and support vector machines (Unit 3) is an inverse $\lambda$; leaf size of a tree (Unit 4) and weight decay of a network (Unit 6) play the same role. In QSAR (BGM324), with hundreds of descriptors and a few dozen molecules, $p > n$ and ridge and its relatives (lasso, elastic net, partial least squares) are the only way to fit a linear model at all. Theory: Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, chapter 3.[26]

9. Logistic regression: the first classifier

9.1 From a linear score to a probability

The simplest classifier reuses the linear model: a score $z = \mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta$, benign if $z > 0$, as in Figure 3. But a score is not a probability, and fitting it by least squares to labels 0 and 1 predicts 1.4 or −0.2 and is pulled around by cases already far on the correct side. Logistic regression passes the score through the sigmoid:

$$p(\mathbf{x}) = P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta}}$$ $\sigma(0) = 0.5$, $\sigma(z) \to 1$ as $z \to \infty$, $\sigma(-z) = 1 - \sigma(z)$. Inverting: $\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta = \log\frac{p}{1-p}$ — the score is the log-odds (logit), each coefficient is a change in log-odds per unit of its feature, and $e^{\beta_j}$ is an odds ratio, the quantity reported in every clinical paper that uses the model.

The boundary at threshold 0.5 is still the hyperplane $\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta = 0$; the sigmoid adds a calibrated statement of how far from it a case is. The regression formulation with maximum-likelihood fitting is Cox's (1958).[27]

# The sigmoid function and its derivative.
sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
z = np.linspace(-8, 8, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
ax.plot(z, sigmoid(z), color=BLUE, lw=2, label=r"$\sigma(z) = 1 / (1 + e^{-z})$")
ax.plot(z, sigmoid(z) * (1 - sigmoid(z)), color=ORANGE, lw=1.5, ls="--", label=r"derivative $\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$")
ax.axhline(0.5, color=GREY, lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8)
for zz in [-4, -2, 0, 2, 4]:
    ax.plot(zz, sigmoid(zz), "o", color=BLUE, ms=5); ax.annotate(f"{sigmoid(zz):.3f}", (zz, sigmoid(zz)), xytext=(4, -10), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("linear score z (log-odds)"); ax.set_ylabel("probability"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="center left")
ax.set_title("The sigmoid maps any score to a probability"); fig.tight_layout()

Figure 11. The sigmoid and its derivative. A score of 0 is probability 0.5; ±2 gives 0.88 and 0.12; ±4 gives 0.98 and 0.02. The derivative is largest at the boundary and vanishes far from it, so training is driven by cases near the boundary, not by confidently classified ones.

9.2 The loss: log-loss

Maximum likelihood replaces least squares: choose the parameters under which the observed labels were most probable. The training set had probability $\prod_i p_i^{y_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - y_i}$; one minimises its negative logarithm, the log-loss (binary cross-entropy):

$$L(\boldsymbol\beta) = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - p_i) \,\Big], \qquad p_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)$$ A benign case ($y_i = 1$) predicted at $p_i = 0.9$ contributes $-\log 0.9 \approx 0.105$; at $p_i = 0.1$, $2.3$; as $p_i \to 0$, an unbounded penalty. Confident wrong predictions are punished without limit, which keeps the probabilities honest.

Its gradient has the form of Section 7.3 — $\nabla L = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y})$, features times residuals — so gradient descent applies unchanged (Exercise 4), and the loss is convex. But the sigmoid is not linear, so there is no closed form: the first model whose training requires an optimiser (scikit-learn uses L-BFGS).

9.3 Fitting the model on two features

The cell fits the model to mean radius and mean concave points (× 100) on the training split of Figure 4, with regularisation nearly off (C=1e4) so the coefficients are plain maximum-likelihood estimates. The positive class is benign (code 1).

# Logistic regression on two features: coefficients, log-odds interpretation, accuracy and log-loss.
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss
logreg = LogisticRegression(C=1e4, max_iter=5000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)            # same split as Figure 4
b0, (b_rad, b_cp) = logreg.intercept_[0], logreg.coef_[0]
print(f"log-odds(benign) = {b0:.2f} + ({b_rad:.3f}) x radius + ({b_cp:.3f}) x concave points x100   "
      f"[converged in {logreg.n_iter_[0]} iterations]")
print(f"odds ratio per 1 um of radius: {np.exp(b_rad):.2f}  |  per 0.01 of concave points: {np.exp(b_cp):.2f}")
p_te = logreg.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]                                       # P(benign) for the 171 test cases
print(f"test accuracy (threshold 0.5) = {logreg.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}  |  test log-loss = {log_loss(y_te, p_te):.3f}  "
      f"|  log-loss of always predicting the base rate = {log_loss(y_te, np.full_like(p_te, y_tr.mean())):.3f}")

log-odds(benign) = 13.85 + (-0.634) x radius + (-0.890) x concave points x100   [converged in 15 iterations]
odds ratio per 1 um of radius: 0.53  |  per 0.01 of concave points: 0.41
test accuracy (threshold 0.5) = 0.912  |  test log-loss = 0.228  |  log-loss of always predicting the base rate = 0.661

Both coefficients are negative: larger nuclei and more concave points lower the log-odds of benignity. Each additional micrometre of radius multiplies the odds of benignity by 0.53, roughly halving them, all else equal. Test accuracy at threshold 0.5 is 0.912 — that of the nearest-centroid classifier and the lines of Figure 3, as expected of another straight line. New is the log-loss, 0.228 against 0.661 for predicting the base rate: how much better the probabilities are, which accuracy cannot see.

9.4 Worked example by hand: one probability

Round the coefficients to $\beta_0 = 13.8$, $\beta_{\text{radius}} = -0.63$, $\beta_{\text{cp}} = -0.89$ and take the new case of Unit 1, Section 5.1: radius 15 µm, concave points × 100 = 4.

Step 1 — score. $z = 13.8 - 0.63 \times 15 - 0.89 \times 4 = 13.8 - 9.45 - 3.56 = 0.79$.

Step 2 — sigmoid. $e^{-0.79} \approx 0.454$, so $p(\text{benign}) = 1/(1 + 0.454) \approx 0.688$ and $p(\text{malignant}) \approx 0.312$.

Step 3 — decision. At threshold 0.5 the case is benign, as in Unit 1 — but the model now says one chance in three of malignancy, a statement a clinician would act on. A second case, radius 18 and concave points 8: $z = -4.66$, $p(\text{benign}) \approx 0.009$.

# Confirming the hand calculation with the fitted model (unrounded coefficients) and with the rounded ones.
new_cases = np.array([[15.0, 4.0], [18.0, 8.0]])
z_hand = 13.8 - 0.63 * new_cases[:, 0] - 0.89 * new_cases[:, 1]
print("rounded coefficients : z =", z_hand.round(3), " p(benign) =", sigmoid(z_hand).round(3))
print("fitted model         : z =", logreg.decision_function(new_cases).round(3),
      " p(benign) =", logreg.predict_proba(new_cases)[:, 1].round(3), " class =", logreg.predict(new_cases))

rounded coefficients : z = [ 0.79 -4.66]  p(benign) = [0.688 0.009]
fitted model         : z = [ 0.777 -4.683]  p(benign) = [0.685 0.009]  class = [1 0]

Rounded and exact coefficients agree to two decimals. The model outputs the probability; the label is a separate step (Section 9.5).

# The probability surface of the fitted model, its decision boundary, and the 171 test cases.
xx2, yy2 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(6, 30, 300), np.linspace(-1, 22, 300))
P_grid = logreg.predict_proba(np.c_[xx2.ravel(), yy2.ravel()])[:, 1].reshape(xx2.shape)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.9), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.35, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
im = ax.contourf(xx2, yy2, P_grid, levels=np.linspace(0, 1, 11), cmap="RdBu", alpha=0.85)
ax.contour(xx2, yy2, P_grid, levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9], colors="k", linewidths=[0.7, 1.5, 0.7], linestyles=["--", "-", "--"])
for c, col, name in [(0, ORANGE, "malignant"), (1, BLUE, "benign")]:
    ax.scatter(*X_te[y_te == c].T, color=col, s=12, edgecolor="k", linewidth=0.3, label=f"test cases, {name}")
ax.scatter(*new_cases.T, marker="*", s=200, color=GREEN, edgecolor="k", zorder=5, label="hand-worked cases")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="P(benign)"); ax.legend(fontsize=7.5, frameon=False, loc="upper right")
ax.set_xlabel("mean radius (um)"); ax.set_ylabel("mean concave points x 100"); ax.set_title("Probability surface; solid line P = 0.5, dashed P = 0.1 and 0.9")
# probabilities of the test cases, by true class
ax = axes[1]
ax.hist(p_te[y_te == 1], bins=20, range=(0, 1), color=BLUE, alpha=0.7, label="true benign")
ax.hist(p_te[y_te == 0], bins=20, range=(0, 1), color=ORANGE, alpha=0.7, label="true malignant")
ax.axvline(0.5, color="k", lw=1.2); ax.set_xlabel("predicted P(benign)"); ax.set_ylabel("test cases"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Predicted probabilities of the test cases"); fig.tight_layout()

Figure 12. Left: predicted probability of benignity over the feature plane, the boundary $P = 0.5$ (solid) and the lines $P = 0.1$ and $0.9$ (dashed). The boundary is straight; the colours add the band of uncertainty where almost all misclassified cases lie. Stars: the hand-worked cases, one at $P \approx 0.69$, one deep in the red. Right: predicted probabilities of the test cases by true class — most benign above 0.9, most malignant below 0.1, and an overlap in the middle where the cases any threshold will misclassify live.

9.5 The threshold and the cost of errors

The histogram is the whole decision problem. Wherever the threshold sits, malignant cases to its right are called benign (false negatives, missed cancers) and benign cases to its left malignant (false positives, unnecessary biopsies); moving it trades one for the other. The default 0.5 is right only if both errors cost the same. If a missed cancer costs ten times a biopsy, the optimal rule calls malignant whenever $P(\text{malignant}) > 1/11 \approx 0.09$. The cell computes sensitivity, specificity and total cost under a 10 : 1 ratio for every threshold.

# Sensitivity, specificity and total cost as functions of the decision threshold on P(malignant).
p_mal = 1 - p_te; is_mal = (y_te == 0)
thresholds = np.linspace(0.02, 0.98, 97); rows = []
for t in thresholds:
    call_mal = p_mal >= t
    tp, fn = (call_mal & is_mal).sum(), (~call_mal & is_mal).sum()
    fp, tn = (call_mal & ~is_mal).sum(), (~call_mal & ~is_mal).sum()
    rows.append(dict(threshold=t, sensitivity=tp / is_mal.sum(), specificity=tn / (~is_mal).sum(),
                     missed_cancers=fn, unnecessary_biopsies=fp, cost_10_to_1=10 * fn + fp))
tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)
best = tab.loc[tab.cost_10_to_1.idxmin()]
print(f"Among the {len(y_te)} test cases ({is_mal.sum()} malignant): lowest 10:1 cost at threshold {best.threshold:.2f} "
      f"({int(best.missed_cancers)} missed, {int(best.unnecessary_biopsies)} unnecessary biopsies, cost {int(best.cost_10_to_1)})")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.3))
axes[0].plot(tab.threshold, tab.sensitivity, color=ORANGE, label="sensitivity (malignant caught)")
axes[0].plot(tab.threshold, tab.specificity, color=BLUE, label="specificity (benign left alone)")
axes[0].axvline(0.5, color=GREY, ls=":"); axes[0].axvline(best.threshold, color=GREEN, ls="--")
axes[0].set_xlabel("threshold on P(malignant)"); axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); axes[0].set_title("The trade-off between the two error types")
axes[1].plot(tab.threshold, tab.cost_10_to_1, color="k", label="cost = 10 x missed + 1 x unnecessary")
axes[1].plot(tab.threshold, tab.missed_cancers + tab.unnecessary_biopsies, color=GREY, ls="--", label="cost = 1 x missed + 1 x unnecessary")
axes[1].axvline(0.5, color=GREY, ls=":"); axes[1].axvline(best.threshold, color=GREEN, ls="--", label=f"minimum at {best.threshold:.2f}")
axes[1].set_xlabel("threshold on P(malignant)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("total cost on 171 test cases"); axes[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_title("Total cost under two cost ratios"); fig.tight_layout()
tab.iloc[[8, 28, 48, 68, 88]].round(3).set_index("threshold")

Right: total cost under two ratios. With equal costs (dashed) the minimum is near 0.5; with a missed cancer weighted ten times a biopsy (solid) it moves to 0.13 (green), where 2 of 64 cancers are missed at the price of 23 unnecessary biopsies, against 9 missed and 6 unnecessary at 0.5. Model, probability, decision

A probabilistic classifier separates the model (fitted once), the probability (what it knows about a case) and the decision (which depends on costs that are clinical and ethical, not statistical). Decision-curve analysis formalises the threshold choice as net clinical benefit,[28] and calibration — whether cases given $P = 0.3$ are malignant 30 % of the time — must be checked separately from accuracy and is neglected in most published models.[29] Supplement S1 develops both.

9.6 Logistic regression in medicine

The risk scores of daily practice are logistic regressions in disguise. The Framingham risk score for coronary heart disease was fitted to 5,345 participants followed for 12 years; its point tables are coefficients rounded to integers for computation on paper.[30] SAPS II for intensive-care mortality is a logistic regression on 12,997 patients from 137 units, its 17 variables selected and weighted by the regression.[31] The Gail model gives a woman's probability of breast cancer from age, reproductive and family history.[32] Each is a linear score in clinical features, a sigmoid and a threshold that is a clinical decision. The TRIPOD statement specifies how such models must be reported — including the full equation — and is the checklist to apply when you read one.[33]

9.7 More than two classes

One-versus-rest fits $K$ binary models and picks the most confident. Multinomial (softmax) regression fits one score $z_k = \mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_k$ per class and converts them jointly with the softmax:

$$P(y = k \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}}$$ positive, summing to one, and reducing to the sigmoid of the score difference for $K = 2$. The loss is the same log-loss, $-\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \log P(y = y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i)$, and the output layer of every neural-network classifier (Units 6 and 8) is a softmax.

The cell applies it to the handwritten digits of Unit 1 — ten classes, 64 pixels[34] — and shows the confusion matrix.

# Multinomial (softmax) logistic regression on the 1,797 digits: ten classes, 64 pixel features.
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
digits = datasets.load_digits()
Xg_tr, Xg_te, yg_tr, yg_te = train_test_split(digits.data, digits.target, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=digits.target)
softmax_clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, C=0.05)).fit(Xg_tr, yg_tr)
proba = softmax_clf.predict_proba(Xg_te)
print(f"test accuracy on {len(yg_te)} digits = {softmax_clf.score(Xg_te, yg_te):.3f}  |  "
      f"probabilities sum to one: {np.allclose(proba.sum(1), 1)}  |  mean confidence in the chosen class = {proba.max(1).mean():.3f}")
cm = confusion_matrix(yg_te, softmax_clf.predict(Xg_te))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 4.4))
ax.imshow(cm, cmap="Blues"); ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_yticks(range(10))
for i in range(10):
    for j in range(10):
        ax.text(j, i, cm[i, j], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color="w" if cm[i, j] > cm.max() / 2 else "k")
ax.set_xlabel("predicted digit"); ax.set_ylabel("true digit"); ax.set_title("Confusion matrix of softmax regression (540 test digits)")
fig.tight_layout()

test accuracy on 540 digits = 0.963  |  probabilities sum to one: True  |  mean confidence in the chosen class = 0.857

Figure 14. Confusion matrix on 540 held-out digits: rows true, columns predicted, diagonal correct. Accuracy is 0.963 — a linear model on raw pixels misreads one digit in 27 — and the off-diagonal entries show which confusions occur (five 8s read as 1), information accuracy hides and that matters when some confusions are graver than others.
